newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian wharf workers back on the job.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian wharf workers back on the job.

text.p: Australian waterfront workers returned to work at about midnight on Tuesday after walking off the job earlier in the day to protest against new industrial relations laws but the threat of industrial action remained.
The walk-off occurred at the four major Australian ports of Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne and Fremantle.
Further industrial action could be taken, possibly in conjunction with other major unions, said Vic Slater, assistant national secretary of the Maritime Union of Australia (MUA).

"We'll be looking at the whole ... we've got contacts with the AMWU (Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union), the CFMEU (Construction Forestry Mining and Energy Union) and the PTU (Public Transport Union) ... (we're) talking about having an agreement for mutual support," Slater said.
The spontaneous walk-off in was particularly directed at clauses of the Workplace Relations Bill which were felt to be targeted at the MUA.
The Bill was passed in the Senate on Tuesday afternoon.
The clauses refer to primary and secondary boycott provisions. Secondary boycott provisions curb the right to strike by workers not directly involved in a dispute.

Provisions on industrial action in areas involved with international trade and commerce might deny to workers rights which applied to workers in other areas, Slater said. "That can mean the whole transport chain effectively," he said.

"A de facto no-strike provision could be effected in relation to some people deemed to be in an area of the economy where they were required to be at work at all times irrespective of what happened to them," he said.

Slater also said the national coal strike presently being threatened by the CFMEU was not connected with last night's port stoppages. But liaison by MUA with other unions such as CFMEU had already begun, he said.
John Maitland, general president of the CFMEU, told Reuters a meeting would be held on Friday with the MUA to discuss joint opposition to the industrial relations bill.
This could make a national coal strike a possibility regardless of developments in the present dispute over retrenchment pay at Metropolitan Colliery, south of Sydney.
The mine is owned by Denehurst Ltd.
A waterfront workers strike in conjunction with a national coal strike would cripple Australia's commodity export trade, worth an estimated total A$63.6 billion in 1996/97.
